entries.b: Rope imprints on broken pottery shards excavated in China provide the earliest physical evidence of hemp use anywhere in the world. The Chinese called the plant 'ma' and exploited it for fibre, rope, cloth, and grain, establishing a tradition of hemp cultivation that would persist for twelve millennia.
entries.src: Russo (2007), Cannabis and Cannabinoids; general archaeobotanical consensus
entries.flag: Dating based on ceramic impressions; direct hemp fibre samples are somewhat later

entries.t: Shennong Ben Cao Jing: Cannabis as a Superior Herb
entries.b: The Divine Farmer's Classic of Materia Medica, attributed to the legendary Emperor Shennong, classified cannabis ('ma') as a superior, life-prolonging herb treating malaria, rheumatism, constipation, and beri-beri. The text also warned that excess consumption produced 'visions of devils,' the earliest recorded acknowledgment of cannabis psychoactivity in Chinese medicine.
entries.src: Li H-L (1974), Economic Botany; Russo E (2007); Touw M (1981), Journal of Psychoactive Drugs
entries.extract: The fruit of hemp... if taken in excess will produce visions of devils. Over the long term, it makes one communicate with spirits and lightens one's body.

entries.t: Yanghai Shaman Burial — Earliest Cannabis Cache
entries.b: Excavations at the Yanghai Tombs near Turpan, Xinjiang, revealed a 2,700-year-old Caucasoid shaman buried with ~789g of whole female cannabis tops. Phytochemical analysis confirmed THC, cannabinol (proving original psychoactivity), and the THC-synthase enzyme. The deliberate selection of psychoactive material marks this as ritual or medicinal use.
entries.src: Russo EB et al. (2008), Journal of Experimental Botany 59(15): 4171-4182; Jiang H-E et al. (2006), Journal of Ethnopharmacology 108(3)
entries.extract: The cannabis was presumably employed by this culture as a medicinal or psychoactive agent, or an aid to divination.

entries.t: Jirzankal Cemetery — Earliest Documented Cannabis Smoking
entries.b: At the Jirzankal Cemetery on the Pamir Plateau, far-western China, wooden braziers from eight tombs yielded chemical traces of unusually high-THC cannabis, confirmed by GC-MS analysis. Mourners almost certainly inhaled psychoactive vapour in enclosed burial chambers, making this the earliest direct archaeological evidence of intentional cannabis smoking anywhere in the world.
entries.src: Ren M et al. (2019), Science Advances 5(6): eaaw1391. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aaw1391
entries.extract: People may have been [burning cannabis] to communicate with the divine or the dead.

image.caption: Cannabis sativa botanical illustration (Köhler 1887), showing the plant central to Jirzankal ritual

entries.t: Herodotus Documents Scythian Hemp Vapor Baths
entries.b: Greek historian Herodotus recorded how Scythian nomads built felt-draped tent sweat-lodges, tossing hemp seeds on red-hot stones to produce thick psychoactive steam after funerals. Pazyryk-culture kurgans in Siberia's Altai Mountains — excavated 1947 — confirmed his account exactly: tent frames, bronze cauldrons of hemp seeds, and heated stones.
entries.src: Herodotus, Histories Book IV ch. 73-75 (Rawlinson trans.); Rudenko SI (1970), Frozen Tombs of Siberia
entries.extract: The Scythians take some of this hemp-seed, and, creeping under the felt coverings, throw it upon the red-hot stones; immediately it smokes, and gives out such a vapour as no Grecian vapour-bath can exceed; the Scyths, delighted, shout for joy.

image.caption: Map of Scythia and Parthia c. 100 BCE, showing the vast steppe corridor of Scythian cannabis ritual

entries.y: c. 1500–1000 BCE (text); psychoactive use documented from c. 11th–13th cent. CE
entries.t: Bhang in the Atharva Veda and Shaivite Hinduism
entries.b: The Atharva Veda names cannabis ('bhanga') among five sacred plants that 'deliver us from woe.' Over subsequent millennia it became inseparable from Shiva worship: sadhus smoke ganja as sacrament, bhang drinks are distributed at Mahashivaratri, and the Himalayan foothills produce charas resin. The Indian Hemp Drugs Commission (1894) documented this tradition across 1,193 interviews in 30 cities.
entries.src: Griffith RTH (1895), Hymns of the Atharva Veda; Indian Hemp Drugs Commission (1894); Sharma et al. (2023), PMC10011848
entries.extract: Bhang is the joy-giver, the sky-flier, the heavenly guide, the poor man's heaven, the soother of grief.
entries.flag: The intoxicating properties of bhang are not clearly described in Sanskrit texts until the medieval period; the Vedic bhanga identification with psychoactive cannabis is accepted but not unanimous

image.caption: Shiva and Parvati prepare bhang, c. 1810-20, Pahari school painting, northern India
image.credit: Unknown Indian artist, Pahari school; Wikimedia Commons

entries.t: Sheikh Haydar and Sufi Hashish in Persia
entries.b: Egyptian historian al-Maqrizi (d. 1442) recorded the legend that Sufi saint Qutb al-Din Haydar (d. 1221 CE), based in Khorasan, discovered hashish during a desert walk and introduced it to his dervish order. Haydariyya Sufis consumed hashish before ritual self-mortification performances. Persian Sufis also drank cannabis in 'dugh-e vahdat' (the drink of unity with God). Pre-Islamic Zoroastrian texts had already called cannabis 'shahdaneh' — the royal seed.
entries.src: al-Maqrizi (14th-15th c.); al-Jawbari (13th c.), Kashf al-Asrar; Rosenthal F (1971), The Herb: Hashish versus Medieval Muslim Society
entries.extract: He told us to take a leaf and eat it, which we did. Then, we returned to the monastery, finding in our hearts an irrepressible joy and gladness.
entries.flag: The Haydar legend is considered apocryphal; hashish was documented in Egypt a century before his lifetime

entries.b: The Mahakala Tantra, a key Vajrayana Buddhist text, incorporates cannabis (leaves and resin) in 42 of 50 chapters as a medicinal and ritual plant aiding health, wisdom, and meditative depth. The Tibetan Dictionary of Materia Medica lists cannabis as a rasayana (rejuvenating elixir). Esoteric traditions held that large doses heightened awareness during Tantric ceremony.
entries.src: Stablein WG (1976), The Mahakala Tantra, Columbia Univ. dissertation; Parker & Lux, Psychoactive Plants in Tantric Buddhism
entries.flag: Mainstream Tibetan Buddhism prohibits intoxicants under the Fifth Precept; Tantric cannabis use was confined to specific esoteric lineages

entries.t: Indian Hemp Drugs Commission: Colonial Science Confronts Ancient Tradition
entries.b: The British Indian Government commissioned a 7-volume, 3,281-page report interviewing 1,193 doctors, sadhus, yogis, army officers, and hemp dealers across 30 cities. It concluded that moderate bhang use was the rule rather than the exception, caused 'no appreciable injury,' and recommended taxation rather than prohibition — one of the most comprehensive cannabis policy studies ever conducted.
entries.src: Indian Hemp Drugs Commission Report (1894), Government of India; Hall W (2019), Addiction doi: 10.1111/add.14640
entries.extract: The moderate use practically produces no ill effects. In all but the most exceptional cases, the injury from habitual moderate use is not appreciable.

image.caption: Hemp drug shop in Kandesh (Maharashtra), 1894 — photograph from the Indian Hemp Drugs Commission Report, showing bhang, ganja, and majum for sale
image.credit: Indian Hemp Drugs Commission (British Indian Government, 1894); Wikimedia Commons

facts: The Yanghai shaman's cannabis cache weighed ~789 grams and still contained detectable THC after 2,700 years in desert sand — the largest ancient psychoactive cannabis find ever excavated (Russo et al. 2008).

Herodotus's description of Scythian hemp vapor baths (440 BCE) was confirmed archaeologically 2,400 years later when Rudenko (1947) excavated Pazyryk kurgans and found the exact tent frames and hemp-seed cauldrons Herodotus described.
The English word 'canvas' descends from Latin 'cannabis' — hemp fibre was so dominant in textile and sailcloth production that the material took the plant's name across European languages.

Bhang remains technically legal in India today because the 1985 Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act bans cannabis resin (charas) and flowering tops but not leaves — a loophole rooted directly in the 1894 Hemp Drugs Commission's finding that bhang caused 'no appreciable harm'.

The Jirzankal cemetery sits above 3,000 metres altitude in the Pamirs; cannabis plants at high altitude produce more THC as UV-protection, which may explain why the Jirzankal strains showed elevated THC far above typical wild cannabis (Ren et al. 2019).

Sheikh Haydar allegedly swore his disciples to secrecy about the location of the cannabis fields, sharing the secret only with 'the destitute dervishes of God' — a detail recorded by al-Maqrizi more than a century after Haydar's death, suggesting legendary accretion (Rosenthal 1971).

Nepalese Temple Balls — spherical hand-rolled charas from the Himalayan foothills — were described by botanist Francis Buchanan-Hamilton in 1819 as the finest cannabis resin available anywhere in the world, and they remain a benchmark in global hashish culture.

The Mahakala Tantra includes cannabis in 42 of its 50 chapters — more than any other single plant — yet mainstream Tibetan Buddhist institutions prohibit cannabis use under the Fifth Precept against intoxicants, revealing a deep internal tension within the tradition (Stablein 1976).
